extracted.intended_audience: military officers and informed public interested in frontier/colonial warfare tactics
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive observations and operational recommendations for conducting small‑war, mountain and frontier campaigns (logistics, intelligence, weapons, tactics, signalling, and force composition). Drawn from first‑hand campaign experience and illustrated with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of civil and military duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil officers should discharge diplomatic duties, and military officers the conduct of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues civil officers should not be expected to understand what kind of military information a general requires. Diplomatic tasks belong to civil officers; the conduct of war (including collection and use of military intelligence) belongs to military officers. Example: scanty civil-sourced information on the Mamunds contributed to heavy losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political officers subordinate to the General
rubrics_metrics.description: The political officers must be under the control of the General directing the operations. There must be no 'Imperium in imperio.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid empowering political officers to make arrangements with tribesmen without consulting or informing the commander, because such independent action can create differences that endanger the campaign and soldiers' lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military responsibility for intelligence collection
rubrics_metrics.description: The collection of information as to the numbers and intentions of the enemy would be better and more appropriately carried out by the Intelligence Department and the cavalry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Pathan Sepoys, the Intelligence Branch, and enterprising cavalry to obtain facts required by a general. Assigning intelligence to military organs makes responsibility definite and better fits operational needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport is the paramount consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The first and most important consideration is transport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An army is a ponderous mass requiring long chains of depots and communications; in roadless valleys wheeled traffic is impossible and moving supplies is enormously difficult and costly. Logistics planning must dominate operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer mule transport to camels; avoid mixing
rubrics_metrics.description: Mule transport is for many reasons superior to camel transport. The mule moves faster and can traverse more difficult ground. To mix the two—camels and mules—appears to combine the disadvantages of both, and destroy the superiority of either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mobility is needed (e.g., brigade movement), equip with mules. Consider equipping brigades entirely with mules for rapid movement and availability for sudden operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrenchment layout: ditch toward the enemy and hold higher ground
rubrics_metrics.description: It is thought advisable to have the ditch of the entrenchment towards the enemy. Modern weapons notwithstanding, the ultimate appeal is to the bayonet, and the advantage of being on the higher ground is then considerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In night firing and where assaults and sword rushes occur, position entrenchments to favor bayonet use and elevation. Tactical earthwork placement should anticipate close-quarters fighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infantry placement when artillery forms part of camp line
rubrics_metrics.description: When a battery forms part of the line round a camp, infantry soldiers should be placed between the guns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite artillery officers' objections, mixed placement reduces vulnerabilities—do not over-estimate the power of any single arm; combine arms for mutual protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marksmanship allowance and bayonet emphasis in broken terrain
rubrics_metrics.description: Against quickly moving riflemen in broken ground, better results were obtained by picking out good shots and giving them permission to fire when they saw their opportunity... infantry should push on to the attack with the bayonet without wasting much time in firing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely less on volley fire in rocky hollows; empower skilled marksmen to take opportunistic shots. Infantry should prioritize bayonet assaults rather than prolonged firing when closing with a well-posted, mobile enemy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to carry away wounded and impact on fighting strength
rubrics_metrics.description: To carry away the wounded is a sacred duty... it takes at least four men, and very often more, to carry away a body. Observe the result. Every man hit, means five rifles withdrawn from the firing line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carrying wounded and dead imposes severe reductions in combat power and creates targets for the enemy. Commanders must plan for evacuation manpower and the tactical consequences of casualties during retirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masked, covered and continuous retirements
rubrics_metrics.description: All retirements should be masked by leaving two or three men behind from each company. These keep up a brisk fire, and after the whole company have taken up a new position, or have nearly done so, they run back and join them... the fire of one company in retiring should always be arranged to cover another, and at no moment in a withdrawal should the firing ever cease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange overlapping covering fires; ensure covering company is in position and firing before rear begins to move; use alternating retirements and cross-fire (example: Guides Infantry and Major Campbell's retirement) to minimize casualties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and leverage new small arms (Lee‑Metford and Dum‑Dum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of the new Lee‑Metford rifle with the new Dum‑Dum bullet... its stopping power is all that could be desired... the improved bullet... on striking a bone... spreads out, and... causes wounds which in the body must be generally mortal and in any limb necessitate amputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the ballistic and terminal effects of weapons in theatre; anticipate psychological and medical consequences. Note legal queries from continental critics (Geneva/St. Petersburg Conventions) but author states no clause forbids expansive bullets; use weapons that perform effectively in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers should not be conspicuous in dress
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity for having the officers in the same dress as the men, was apparent... the conspicuous figure which a British officer in his helmet presented in contrast to the native soldiers... drew a well‑aimed fire in his direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce visual markers (distinctive helmets, equipment) that identify officers; officers should blend with troops where possible to avoid being singled out by sharpshooters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lighten soldier's load and prioritize ammunition accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The fatigues experienced by troops in mountain warfare are so great, that every effort has to be made to lighten the soldier's load. At the same time the more ammunition he carries on his person the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce unnecessary heavy leather equipment (consider webbing despite wear) and ensure cartridges are carried on person rather than on pack animals that may be lost; plan for equipment replacement at base rather than burdening soldiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide portable, nutritious rations for soldiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Great efforts should be made to give the soldier a piece of chocolate, a small sausage, or something portable and nutritious to carry with him to the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate long marches and nights out without food; small high‑energy portable items sustain morale and performance. 'The stomach governs the world.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate artillery even in mountain warfare
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of concentrating artillery has long been admitted in Europe. Sir Bindon Blood is the first general who has applied it to mountain warfare in India... the fire of this artillery drove the enemy... The infantry attack was accomplished with hardly any loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where practical, mass guns to achieve decisive effects rather than dispersing them in twos or threes; concentration can enable infantry success with fewer casualties. Apply concentration thoughtfully in mountain operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artillery's role: limitations and use to deny ground
rubrics_metrics.description: After this, it may seem strange if I say that the artillery fire in the Mamund Valley did very little execution... Where they really were of great service, was not so much in killing the enemy, but in keeping them from occupying certain spurs and knolls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize artillery's limited lethality against sharpshooters in broken rocky ground; instead use guns to deny key terrain and prevent enemy occupation. In rearguard actions artillery is imperative; at least two batteries should accompany a brigade to the attack if available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signalling by heliograph and semi‑permanent signal lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Signalling by heliograph was throughout the operations of the greatest value... as soon as any hill was taken, communication was established with the brigadier... In this torrid country, where the sun is always shining, the heliograph is always useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish semi‑permanent lines of signal stations along communications to the telegraph; heliograph provides the surest and quickest means of intercommunication in sunlit, ravine‑intersected terrain where ground movement is slow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cavalry armament and organisation: favour the lance and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: All admit or assert that the lance is in this warfare the better weapon. As to length, the general opinion seems to be in favour of a shorter spear... Either the pennon should be knotted, or a boss of some sort affixed... In considering the question to what extent a squadron should be armed with lances... The Guides compromise matters by giving one man in every four a lance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer shorter lances with counterpoise and pennon modifications to prevent over‑penetration. Organise squadrons so a proportion keep lances (e.g., 1 in 4); when others dismount, lance‑holders remain mounted to hold horses. Balance lance utility with dismounting requirements and skirmishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous 'dash' — favour cautious, purposeful command
rubrics_metrics.description: The general who avoids all 'dash,' who never starts in the morning looking for a fight and without any definite intention, who does not attempt heroic achievements, and who keeps his eye on his watch, will have few casualties and little glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise measured operations with clear objectives and timing. Avoid seeking action for its own sake; mistakes, not the enemy's intrinsic strength, make the enemy formidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment and service policy: favour quality over quantity for frontier needs
rubrics_metrics.description: We have adopted the 'short service' system... We have got the poor quality, without the great quantity... Our soldiers are not required to operate in great masses... They are sent beyond the seas... Boys of twenty‑one and twenty‑two are expected to compete on equal terms with Sikhs and Gurkhas of thirty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For colonial/frontier campaigns prefer older, better‑trained soldiers (longer service) rather than short‑service recruits; if large conscript armies are not desired, maintain higher quality through recruitment/training to meet the rigours of individual combat in harsh climates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for native regiments' experience and the morale consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The native regiments are ten years older than the British regiments. Many of their men have seen service and have been under fire... It is evident how many advantages they enjoy. It is also apparent how very serious the consequences would be if they imagined they possessed any superiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and value the experience and stamina of native/regional troops (age, prior service, acclimatisation). Manage perceptions and relations carefully to avoid morale or political problems arising from perceived superiority.
